ABSTRACT
Errors in LLM agent executions and their visible consequences can be separated
by many steps, making decisive-error localization a matter of understanding both
step content and step dependencies. We introduce DeFA, a dependency-guided
framework for agent failure attribution. DeFA first combines protocol relations
and semantic dependencies into an event dependency graph spanning the trajec-
tory. It then identifies events that may violate task requirements and traces their
sources and subsequent effects to construct a failure propagation graph. Finally,
DeFA uses step evidence and the steps’ roles in failure propagation to identify the
decisive error, responsible agent, and error category. To support long trajectories,
DeFA partitions executions into segments and combines the current segment’s
detailed content with summaries of the other segments, giving local diagnosis ac-
cess to global execution context. Across Who&When and the Who&When Pro
text subset, DeFA achieves the highest responsible-agent and exact step accu-
racy with all evaluated backbones, and the highest failure-mode accuracy among
taxonomy-aligned methods on Pro. Further experiments on image and video tra-
jectories demonstrate its applicability to multimodal failure attribution. Ablations
support the contributions of segmentation, the event dependency graph, and the
failure propagation graph. Using DeFA’s diagnostic feedback for skill evolution in
Trace2Skill improves downstream task accuracy by 6–15 percentage points over
the native pipeline, showing that the diagnoses can also support agent improve-
ment on subsequent tasks.

4.4 TRAJECTORY LENGTH ANDLLMCALLS
Localization gains across trajectory lengths.Figure 2a,b shows exact Step accuracy across tra-
jectory lengths with GLM-5.2. Accuracy generally declines as trajectories grow longer, but DeFA
outperforms the baselines in every length interval on both benchmarks. The largest gains occur at
intermediate lengths: DeFA reaches 45.8% on Who&When trajectories of 11–32 steps, exceeding
the strongest baseline by 12.5 percentage points, and improves accuracy by 18.3 points on Pro tra-
jectories of 6–8 steps (67.6% versus 49.3%). These results show that DeFA’s overall improvement
spans different trajectory lengths. Nevertheless, its accuracy remains only 17.2% in the longest
Who&When interval of 33–130 steps despite leading the baselines, indicating that exact localiza-
tion in long trajectories remains challenging.

5 CONCLUSION ANDLIMITATIONS
We introduced DeFA, which traces agent failures through step dependencies. It combines proto-
col relations and semantic dependencies into an event dependency graph spanning the trajectory to
capture how steps use earlier information. DeFA then identifies events that may violate task require-
ments and traces their sources and effects to construct a failure propagation graph. Final attribution
uses this connected evidence to compare how steps introduce, transmit, or adopt errors and identify
the decisive error and responsible agent.
Experiments on Who&When and Who&When Pro demonstrate precise attribution gains across
backbones, trajectory lengths, and text and multimodal inputs. Ablations support segmentation,
the event dependency graph, and the failure propagation graph. DeFA’s diagnostic feedback also
improves test accuracy after Trace2Skill skill evolution by an average of 9.0 percentage points over
the native pipeline, showing that the diagnoses can guide skill improvements for subsequent tasks.
Limitations.DeFA’s semantic dependency recovery and failure propagation analysis depend on
the model’s trajectory interpretation; missing or misidentified relations can affect attribution, es-
pecially in long executions with dispersed evidence. Downstream utility has been evaluated for
spreadsheet skill evolution; effectiveness in other domains and forms of agent improvement remains
to be assessed. Future work can improve relation identification in long trajectories and broaden the
applications of diagnostic feedback.
